To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have demonstrated that the redox activity of pure metal single-sites can be harnessed to form thermally stable, well-defined, one-dimensional polymeric chains on single-crystal gold surfaces.

single-site divalent metals from the 4d and 3d transition metal series can be stabilized at the surface in a redox-active oxidation state, and that they can be assembled into well-defined, polymeric, redox-active chains.
single-site metal cations from the pure metals Fe, Cr, and Pt can be oxidized by a ketone-containing phenanthroline and polymerize into one-dimensional chains on the surface of single crystal gold.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new materials and the study of their physical properties, in particular their electronic structure and chemical reactivity.
the synthesis, characterization, and applications of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and metal-organic polymers.
the synthesis of new molecular systems that can be assembled into well-defined, one-dimensional structures on surfaces, and the study of the electronic and magnetic properties of these structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of a single-site metal, a redox-active ligand and an inert support surface is a viable route to create new materials with tailored redox and catalytic properties.
we have demonstrated a redox-active on-surfacerelated, single-site, polymerization of pure metals by a phenanthroline-based ligand, which is an unprecedented result.
the redox-active on-surfaced polymerization of single site divalent cations is possible from pure metals by the use of a ketone-functionalised phenanthroline.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that a ketone group can be used to bind a metal ion to a surface in a well-defined oxidation-state, and that the resulting metal ion complex can then be polymerized by a second metal ion to form one-dimensional, polymeric structures.

the combination of the ketone and phenanthroline moieties in a single ligand provides the ability to form well-defined metal complexes at the surface, which can be oxidized to the corresponding cations.
a ketone-functional phenanthroline can be used as a ligand to stabilize a transition metal single-site on a single-crystal gold surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a ketone group can be used to stabilize transition metal sites at surfaces.
the redox chemistry is driven by the ligand and not by the metal.
the combination of a single-site metal and a well-defined, redox-active ligand can lead to a well-defined, one-dimensional, polymeric structure that is thermally stable.
